case_name: Lila Dhar v State Of Rajasthan & Ors.
facts: The Rajasthan Public Service Commission held a competitive examination for recruitment of Munsifs.
The competitive examination consisted of a written examination and a viva voce examination.

The viva voce examination was conducted by a Board consisting of Hon'ble Mr. Justice P.D. Kudal, Judge, Rajasthan High Court, Shri Hari Datt Gupta, Chairman, Rajasthan Public Service Commission, Adaviappa, Member, Rajasthan Public Service Commission and an expert.
The result of the competitive examination was announced by the Rajasthan Public Service Commission on March 12, 1981 and respondent Nos. 3 to 41 were declared selected for appointment.
The petitioner who obtained a total of 189 marks, 159 in the written test and 30 in the viva voce was not selected for appointment.
issues: What is the ideal mode of selection to a Public Service?
Is the oral test so pernicious in practice that it should be abandoned without regrets or the weight to be attached to it be made minimal?
petitioner_arguments: The allocation of 25 percent of the total marks for the viva voce examination introduced an irredeemable element of arbitrariness.
Marks were awarded in the interview-test in a single lot instead of sub dividing and awarding marks separately under various heads for the various matters tested in the interview.
court_reasoning: The ideal in recruitment is to do away with unfairness. Competitive examinations were the answer to the twin problems represented by democracy and the requirements of good administration.
Open competitive examinations are a peculiarly democratic institution. Any qualified person may come forward.

A system of recruitment almost totally dependent on assessment of a person's academic knowledge and skills, as distinct from ability to deal with pressing problems of economic and social development, with people, and with novel situations cannot serve the needs of today, much less of tomorrow..

We venture to suggest that our recruitment procedures should be such that we can select candidates who can not only assimilate knowledge and sift material to understand the ramifications of a situation or a problem but have the potential to develop an original or innovative approach to the solution of problems.
holding: The selection cannot be struck down on the ground that more than due weightage was given to the interview test.

There cannot be any magic formulae in these matters and courts cannot sit in judgment over the methods of marking employed by interviewing bodies unless, as we said, it is proven or obvious that the method of marking was chosen with oblique motive.

The Court intended no wide construction of their observation. As already observed by us the weight to be given to the interview test should depend on the requirement of the service to which recruitment is made, the source material available for recruitment, the composition of the interview Board and several like factors.

Ordinarily recruitment to public services is regulated by rules made under the proviso to Art. 309 of the Constitution and we would be usurping a function which is not ours, if we try to redetermine the appropriate method of selection and the relative weight to be attached to the various tests.
